title: New aluminium housing for commercial EV batteries - electrive.com
content:
An aluminium battery housing solution for commercial electric vehicles has been developed by Novelis and Maxion Structural Components. The product was developed from stamped, rolled aluminium using a new alloy specially created for the batteries of heavy duty vehicles such as buses and trucks. The new technology is both lighter and more is able to provide more energy density that previous materials.
Image: screenshot of Novelis recycled aluminium roll
Novelis and Maxion Structural Components have teamed up to creat an aluminium battery housing solution called
Maxion InVolt
, that can be adapted to different vehicle sizes, from light to heavy commercial vehicles. The partners say the new solution is 35 per cent lighter compared to an extruded aluminium housing with the same technical requirements, but still manages to deliver 11 per cent more energy density.
Marco Tulio Ricci, Global Director of Innovation and Engineering at Maxion Structural Components, said: “The development of this solution represents a crucial step in our strategy to reduce the weight of electric commercial vehicles and, consequently, contribute to reducing CO₂ emissions without compromising vehicle load capacity.”
“Not to mention, the metal has enormous circularity potential, being infinitely recyclable, which results in lower energy consumption and less greenhouse gas emissions – up to a 95% reduction.”
Novelis is a subsidiary of Hindalco Industries Limited, an industry leader in aluminum and copper and the metals flagship of the Aditya Birla Group, a multinational conglomerate based in Mumbai, India. Novelis calls itself “a leading sustainable aluminum solutions supplier and a world leader in aluminum recycling and rolling.” In
2022, Novelis invested in battery
startup company Addionics.

title: 7 North American Battery Recycling Companies Scaling in 2026
content:
Battery Recycling
Battery News
These recyclers are adding capacity as new federal rules push end-of-life battery material toward domestic refining.
August 31, 2026
7 Slides
Start slideshow
Inside Redwood Materials' South Carolina facility
Redwood Materials
For most of the lithium-ion era, North America had very limited battery refining capacity. While facilities with shredders and sorting lines could turn used packs into black mass, almost all of that powder had to be sent to refiners in Asia. Because refining capacity lived overseas, recycling economics rose and fell with freight rates and cobalt prices instead of with battery demand at home.
Today, gigafactories in the US Battery Belt continuously generate manufacturing scrap, and the first large wave of EV packs sold in the late 2010s is starting to reach retirement. Together, those streams give recyclers a feedstock volume that finally justifies building hydrometallurgical refineries on this continent. Cell makers also need recycled nickel, cobalt, and lithium with documented domestic origin to qualify for federal incentives, which gives refined output a buyer before it leaves the plant.
Related:
DOE Announces Lithium-Ion Recycling Prize Winners
In 2026, policy has begun to shape around this trend. For example,
a presidential determination
gave the Commerce Department authority to restrict exports of black mass and other critical minerals, with the stated goal of keeping end-of-life battery material inside US borders. Weeks later, t
he Department of Energy named recycling and refining projects
in a $500 million grant round.
As the US embraced domestic refining, we've put together a list of seven battery recycling companies scaling up operations in North America. Read on to learn about their facilities, capacities, and the technologies behind them.

title: NeoVolta, SK On Sign $1B Battery Deal for U.S. Energy Storage
content:
Stationary Batteries
Battery News
Battery Manufacturing
Five-year, $1 billion-plus collaboration establishes end-to-end US supply chain for utility and commercial energy storage systems.
August 31, 2026
5 Min Read
SK Battery America's facility in Commerce, GA.
SK Battery America
At a Glance
$1.09 billion deal supplies 18 GWh of U.S.-made LFP cells from SK On's Georgia factory through 2031
NeoVolta Power targets 8 GWh annual BESS production capacity by 2028 for utility, commercial, and data center markets
All-domestic supply chain positions partnership to meet evolving OBBBA domestic content requirements
NeoVolta Inc. and South Korean battery giant SK On have announced a five-year strategic collaboration valued at approximately $1.09 billion that will supply 18 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for energy storage systems manufactured in Georgia, marking one of the largest domestic battery supply agreements since the passage of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA).
The deal, announced August 31 by both companies, establishes a two-phase partnership: an initial signed agreement for SK On to supply 9 GWh of U.S.-manufactured LFP cells to NeoVolta Power from 2027 through 2031, plus a framework for an additional 9 GWh arrangement under which NeoVolta Power will manufacture battery packs for purchase by SK On over the same period.
"This collaboration represents an important milestone in NeoVolta's expansion into large-scale energy storage and the continued buildout of our U.S. manufacturing platform," stated Ardes Johnson, Chief Executive Officer of NeoVolta, in the company's announcement.
Related:
Cummins Wins Its Largest BESS Contract for US Data Center Project
Ardes Johnson, CEO of NeoVolta. Credit: NeoVolta
Strategic timing: From residential roots to utility scale
The announcement represents a dramatic acceleration of a strategy Johnson outlined to Battery Technology just three months ago. In a
May 2026 interview
Battery Technology
, the CEO emphasized that NeoVolta's domestic manufacturing roadmap "predates the OBBBA," explaining that the company had "long planned to establish US-based manufacturing across the full storage spectrum — from residential systems through the often underserved commercial and industrial 'middle market,' and into utility-scale storage."
That vision is now materializing at commercial scale. The SK On partnership will supply pouch-type LFP cells produced at SK On's Georgia factory to NeoVolta Power's Pendergrass, Georgia facility, which manufactures battery energy storage systems (BESS) for commercial, industrial, and utility-scale applications. According to the company's announcement, the collaboration is expected to accelerate NeoVolta Power's expansion to a two-line manufacturing platform targeting up to 8 GWh of annual BESS production capacity by 2028.
NeoVolta’s NV Wave modular click-in residential ESS. Credit: NeoVolta
The deal validates Johnson's earlier assertion about building ecosystems, not just products. "What truly shortens deployment timelines is building the ecosystem around it," he told Battery Technology in May. "That means working with developers, community choice aggregators, utilities, and program operators that need reliable technology partners and a consistent supply of systems to scale their programs."
Related:
7 Residential Battery Storage Systems Worth Buying in 2026
SK On and ESS as EV hedge
For SK On, the NeoVolta partnership represents a strategic hedge against weakening electric vehicle demand. According to
, "the agreement comes as SK On expands into the energy storage system business to offset weaker demand for electric vehicles."
"This partnership strengthens SK On's position in the US BESS market and brings together SK On's U.S.-made LFP battery technology with NeoVolta Power's growing energy storage manufacturing capabilities," stated Daejin Choi, Head of ESS Business at SK On, in the joint announcement.
SK On had set a target of securing more than 20 GWh of global energy storage system orders this year and is in talks with several U.S. customers over additional supply contracts totaling more than 10 GWh, according to
. Competitors including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are also repurposing EV battery production lines for energy storage as U.S. EV subsidies phase out.
LFP chemistry as insulation from commodity volatility
NeoVolta's commitment to lithium iron phosphate chemistry—rather than nickel-manganese-cobalt formulations—provides strategic insulation from raw material price volatility, a consideration Johnson emphasized in our
May interview
Related:
Understanding Base Power’s role in energy storage solutions
"Our use of lithium iron phosphate chemistry helps avoid exposure to nickel and cobalt volatility, while our US assembly platform improves logistics, quality control, and alignment with domestic content incentives," Johnson explained. He added that the company is "preparing for where policy and market requirements are headed," noting that "as domestic content thresholds and FEOC [Foreign Entity of Concern] requirements increase over time, we anticipate the industry moving further upstream."
The all-domestic supply chain—SK On's Georgia-manufactured cells paired with NeoVolta Power's Georgia-based pack assembly—positions the collaboration to meet evolving domestic content requirements under OBBBA. As the release notes, "by pairing US-manufactured LFP cells with US-based BESS manufacturing, [NeoVolta] believes its platform is positioned to serve customers seeking reliable and domestic content BESS solutions."
The deal arrives as the energy storage industry undergoes fundamental repositioning. As Johnson told Battery Technology in May, "the industry conversation is shifting from simply pairing solar with storage to recognizing that storage itself is the primary grid asset, with solar as an optional generation source layered on top."
This philosophical shift—from viewing batteries as backup devices to treating them as dispatchable, revenue-generating grid infrastructure—underpins the commercial logic of multi-gigawatt-hour supply agreements. The target markets reflect this evolution: according to the press release, the partnership targets "utility, commercial, industrial, AI data-center markets." The inclusion of AI data centers is particularly notable, reflecting explosive growth in power-intensive computing infrastructure.
Production timeline and industry implications
NeoVolta Power's initial Pendergrass production line "remains on track to advance through commissioning and production-ramp activities," with cell deliveries and pack production scheduled to begin in 2027 and continue through 2031.
The NeoVolta-SK On collaboration represents one of the clearest examples to date of how OBBBA and related domestic content incentives are reshaping battery supply chains. Rather than importing finished products from Asia, the partnership establishes an end-to-end domestic value chain: Korean battery technology transferred to U.S. manufacturing, paired with U.S.-based system integration.
This model—foreign technology expertise combined with domestic production—may become a template for other international battery manufacturers seeking to serve the U.S. market while meeting increasingly stringent domestic content requirements.
For NeoVolta, the deal validates the strategic bet Johnson described in May: that focusing on "efficient product design with a growing domestic manufacturing footprint" would position the company as policy shifts toward domestic sourcing.
"We're not only planning for what the supply chain needs today," Johnson told
Battery Technology
. "We're preparing for where policy and market requirements are headed."
With 18 GWh of committed collaboration and a manufacturing platform designed to scale to 8 GWh of annual capacity, NeoVolta and SK On are now positioned to help define what that future looks like.

title: Data Breach & Blind Spots: The Cyber Risk for Supply Chains
content:
Data Breach & Blind Spots: The Cyber Risk for Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Ongoing disruption is exposing more blind spots within supply chain operations. Credit: Getty
As technology becomes more integrated into global supply chains, ongoing disruption is exposing more blind spots within supply chain operations
Around the world, hackers have been targeting organisations in every industry, exposing the vulnerabilities within global supply chains.
Much of this is coming as more organisations are integrating new technologies into their operations, without the necessary risk assessments and understanding of vulnerabilities within their supply chain.
Over the past year, major organisations have been hit, with operations being shut down and consumer details being exposed. With this, supply chain leaders need a greater understanding of their
security systems
Most supply chain disruptions aren’t caused by events no one could have predicted, but rather by vulnerabilities no one previously identified.
Martin Rode, senior consultant at NIRAS
Increasing vulnerabilities
International engineering and management consultancy NIRAS finds that life science and
food and beverage manufacturers
are vulnerable to cyber attacks and other supply chain issues. As ongoing disruption around the world makes organisations vulnerable to shock, more businesses are investing in predictive tools, AI and other digital software.
With this comes a new vulnerability. The more an organisation is reliant on technology – particularly one which is already vulnerable – the more exposed it is to attacks, with increased entry points to its operations and perhaps less security to prevent
breaches
In times of turbulence, technology is being seen as a quick fix. However, digital tools should not be seen as a band-aid to poor decision-making capabilities, particularly when it comes to risk management. Organisations which lack an understanding of how visibility links to resilience put themselves at greater risk when they fail to address blind spots.
“Most supply chain disruptions aren’t caused by events no one could have predicted, but rather by vulnerabilities no one previously identified, whether that’s due to reliance on a single supplier, limited visibility beyond first-tier partners or critical operations concentrated in one geographic location," explains Martin Rode, Senior Consultant at NIRAS.
Martin Rode, senior consultant at NIRAS
“The question for leadership teams  is no longer whether your supply chain will face disruption, but whether they’ve identified the weaknesses that will determine how severely it affects them.”
The risk on logistics
A cyber attack on Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports, has reportedly resulted in the personal data access of approximately 8.7 million customers.
The transport and logistics sector is vulnerable to cyber attacks because it is a deeply integrated, complex and vast network. Throughout the industry, there are a range of suppliers, ageing technology and growing amounts of shared customer data.
As the logistics industry is so vast, with networks spread around the world, attackers have a range of routes they can approach. The sheer amount of entry points also means the breaches are more difficult to contain, with the capability of impacting various companies and regions in one go.
The 2025
JLR cyber attack
was one of the most fitting examples of how a disruption can impact even more businesses, with operations shutting down at a facility and driving losses across a vast network of suppliers.
Thomas Barrett, Partner at Weightmans, says the attack on MAG "is yet another reminder of why cyber security needs to be treated as a standing and fundamental business risk rather than simply an IT issue after the fact, especially within the transport and logistics industries. Prevention is many times better than a cure, and often a cure is impossible and breaches can only be managed".
Thomas Barrett, Partner at Weightmans. Credit: Weightmans
“Businesses understandably invest significant technical resources in preventing
cyber attacks
— but many neglect to plan for what happens if those defences fail or provide similar investment in organisational measures and prevention. Any well-prepared organisation should know who will make critical decisions, how the incident will be contained, which regulators or customers may need to be notified and how essential operations can be restored."
Vetted vendors and scenario modelling
In August, cybercriminal group Clop came out with claims of a data breach impacting almost 50 companies, with giants like Shell, GE and Philips impacted. According to the group, more than 89GB of data has been stolen from Shell and more than 391GB has been stolen from GE.
Supply chain attacks of this calibre are no longer an exception, but rather an increasingly common occurrence.
“We see blind spots in critical data where companies still can't name which shared platforms would wipe out or expose their core engineering data if breached tomorrow,” explains Anup Kumar, CEO of Optiv Consulting.
“Teams treat third-party software as routine vendor compliance items instead of what they actually are – direct extensions of their own crown jewels."
The reliance of third-party software is increasingly putting organisations at risk – a single breach in the software gains access to data from its customers.
Businesses therefore need to have heavily vetted vendors throughout their operations, with regular security checks throughout.
Leading organisations
also need to put an emphasis on proactive threat modelling, coming up with scenarios for best point of action when an issue does arise.

title: Rivian (RIVN) CFO steps down for GE Vernova amid critical R2 ramp
content:
Rivian R2
Fred Lambert
| Aug 31 2026 - 8:23 am PT
Rivian CFO Claire McDonough is stepping down effective October 30, leaving after nearly six years to become chief financial officer of energy giant GE Vernova.
The departure lands at the most important moment in Rivian’s history — the ramp of the R2, the $45,000-to-$58,000 SUV the entire company is betting on.
McDonough joined Rivian in January 2021 and steered the company through its $13.7 billion IPO in November 2021, still one of the largest US public offerings of the decade. She is relocating to the East Coast to be closer to family, and Rivian says the exit is “not the result of any disagreement.”
Derek Mulvey, Rivian’s VP of Finance, will take over as interim CFO on October 30. Mulvey joined Rivian in 2021 and previously worked at J.P. Morgan. The company says it is running a “comprehensive search” for a permanent CFO, evaluating both internal and external candidates, while McDonough stays on for a two-month transition.
McDonough’s tenure covers Rivian’s entire life as a public company. Beyond the IPO, she helped structure the $5.8 billion
Volkswagen Group joint venture
finalized in November 2024 — the deal that gave Rivian both a cash lifeline and a software-platform customer.
GE Vernova, the power-equipment spinoff, has become one of Wall Street’s favorite AI-and-grid plays, riding surging electricity demand from data centers. For a CFO, it’s a jump from a cash-burning EV startup to a profitable energy incumbent at the center of the AI boom.
Rivian’s stock tells the other side of the story. RIVN debuted at $78 in November 2021 and now trades near $17 — down more than 75% from its IPO price. Shares slipped on the CFO news.
Timing collides with the R2 ramp
The exit comes just as Rivian starts delivering the vehicle that has to work. R2
customer deliveries began in June
, and the company is now scaling production at its Normal, Illinois plant.
Rivian has spent 2026 shoring up its finances for exactly this moment. In July, it
launched a 75-million-share offering to raise roughly $1.5 billion
to fund the R2 push, and its
Q2 2026 earnings
showed revenue up 27% with gross margins improving — early signs the cost structure McDonough helped build is starting to pay off.
The R2 itself,
priced from $57,990 with a $45,000 RWD version coming later
, is aimed squarely at the Tesla Model Y — the best-selling SUV in the world and the vehicle Rivian must take volume from to reach profitability.
Electrek’s Take
Losing your CFO in the middle of a make-or-break product ramp is never ideal, but this reads more like a personal move than a red flag. For comparison, Tesla went through several CEO in a similar period.
McDonough guided Rivian through its IPO, the Volkswagen deal, and a genuinely brutal cash-burn period, and she’s leaving with the R2 finally shipping and margins finally turning the right direction. If you’re going to hand off, this is a defensible moment to do it.

title: I traded my electric motorcycle for a gasoline bike on vacation. It was pretty shocking
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Aug 31 2026 - 7:23 am PT
For the last few weeks, my wife and I have been hopping between islands in the Philippines, and like so many travelers (and locals), we’ve been getting around on small gasoline-powered motorbikes.
It’s a big change from our normal electric steeds back home, and an eye-opening reminder of just how stark the everyday differences truly are.
First of all, no matter what is powering it, a motorcycle or scooter is a fantastic way to travel, whether at home or especially abroad. In this case, these were a great way to travel through a new country.
You can explore tiny villages, pull over at hidden beaches, climb mountain roads, and stop wherever something catches your eye. You can park anywhere, squeeze past stopped traffic, and often take roads or routes that would disallow four-wheeled vehicles.
For many places around the world, motorcycles are simply the standard, normal transportation choice.
[Safety note: I always try to gear up for rides, but my wife caught me here while I was just moving the bike a short distance to the hostel parking area.]
But as much fun as I had on the trip, the experience also reminded me just how different small electric motorcycles can be compared to their fuel-burning cousins.
First of all, I’ll still give gasoline bikes one major win: fueling.
Need gas? It’s everywhere. Sure, there are regular gas stations, but what is even more convenient is how in these types of countries, there are so many little roadside convenience shops that seem to always have recycled liquor bottles filled with gasoline sitting out front. Running low wasn’t something I ever worried about. A couple of dollars later, you’re back on the road. I’ve seen this often in my travels around Asia, and I can’t deny how convenient it is.
That’s still an advantage electric motorcycles don’t universally have, especially in developing regions where charging infrastructure is limited. Sure, we can charge our electric motorbikes just about anywhere there’s an electrical outlet, which is theoretically a big win (there are way more electrical outlets than gas stations), but there aren’t necessarily electrical outlets
available
everywhere. So for a few more years, the distributed gasoline station and/or liquor bottles of gasoline infrastructure still has some advantages.
This nice fellow filled me up with 1.5 liters of Coca-Cola’s finest gasoline
After that, though, I found myself missing almost everything about riding electric.
The first thing I noticed was the vibration.
You don’t really appreciate how much a little single-cylinder engine buzzes until you’ve spent several hours on one. By the end of longer rides, I could still feel the tingling in my hands, arms, and bottom for several minutes after I stopped. The handlebars, the seat, even the foot pegs are constantly humming away beneath you. It’s not unbearable, but after spending years riding smooth electric motorcycles and scooters, it felt strangely primitive.
Then there’s the heat.
Small displacement motorcycles don’t produce huge amounts of power, but they certainly produce plenty of waste heat. Every time I pulled a bottle of water from the storage compartment under the seat, it was practically warm tea. That compartment shares a wall with the engine, turning it into a convenient little warming drawer. There might be an advantage there somewhere in the winter, but I didn’t find it.
This little Yamaha did me right, even if it can’t compete with my Gogoro
I also found myself constantly reminding my wife not to let her ankle drift too close to the exhaust pipe when getting on or off the back of the bike – not a concern I’ve ever had on my electrics.
The noise is another thing many people may gradually stop noticing – until you ride electric again.
These little engines spend much of their lives revving near the top of their RPM range, especially climbing hills or accelerating away from traffic lights. It’s not deafening, but it creates a constant soundtrack that becomes mentally fatiguing over the course of a full day in the saddle. With an electric motorcycle, the ride becomes quieter, making it easier to hear the environment around you, carry on conversations during brief stops, or simply enjoy the scenery.
At one point, I rode through a beautiful forest, but the engine noise certainly overwhelmed the natural wind and bird noises I’m used to hearing when riding on my electrics.
Then there are the little annoyances.
Waiting a few moments for the engine to warm up before setting off. The occasional whiff of gasoline when filling up. Hunting for neutral on the motorbikes and the slight jerkiness of low-speed clutch work in heavy traffic (not a concern on the scooters). Having to remember oil changes, air filters, spark plugs, and all the other routine maintenance that internal combustion engines quietly demand. Fortunately, I didn’t have to deal with any of those maintenance concerns since I was on rental bikes the entire time, but there’s nothing like a hundred moving parts underneath you to remind you that it’s
someone’s
headache, even if not yours.
None of these is a major problem individually. They’re all manageable and overcomable. But together, they remind you how much mechanical baggage we’ve simply accepted for over a century.
Electric motorcycles strip away nearly all of it. Twist the throttle and go. No vibrations, almost no noise, no scorching exhaust, no hot engine between your knees, and dramatically less maintenance. I’ll never forget the first time I showed my brother-in-law the controls on
my LiveWire S2 Del Mar motorcycle
(an 80 hp beast that does 0-60 MPH in 3.1 seconds), to which he remarked, “So it’s basically just a big e-bike?”
“Yeah,” I shrugged. “Basically.”
That’s really all there is to electric two-wheelers. Twist and go – no headaches. Compared to gasoline-powered bikes, e-motorcycles are easy like Sunday morning.
If everyone were going electric, we wouldn’t need those masks
Ironically, the Philippines may actually be one of the places that stands to benefit most from electric two-wheelers. The country already relies heavily on motorcycles for daily transportation. Trips are often relatively short. Air quality in many cities would improve (it was bad enough in Cebu City that my wife and I stopped at a local pharmacy to buy masks, though the smaller islands were much better). And while charging infrastructure still has a long way to go, electricity is ultimately easier to distribute than liquid fuel once the investment is made.
I’m not going to sit here and tell you that my vacation was ruined by riding gasoline motorcycles. Quite the opposite – I loved every minute of exploring the islands on two wheels. It was still a lot of fun, and it’s never a bad idea to practice shifting again to keep skills fresh in case you ever need them.
But every day I climbed back onto another buzzing, vibrating little engine, I found myself thinking the same thing: This is exactly the kind of riding that electric motorcycles were made for.

title: Kia confirms PV7 debut and previews the larger electric van for the first time [Video]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 31 2026 - 7:05 am PT
Kia is preparing to launch its second fully electric van following the PV5’s success. With its debut less than a month away,
offered a first look at the larger PV7.
When will the Kia PV7 make its debut?
The PV5 is already the
best-selling small electric van
in Europe, accounting for 37% of the market through the first half of the year.
In five countries, it accounts for more than 50% of C-segment EV van sales. Through August, Kia sold 39,000 PV5s globally. While Kia continues introducing new PV5 variants, it’s preparing to launch the second model from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup.
We knew the PV7 would go on sale sometime in 2027, but Kia finally confirmed its official debut date.
Kia will unveil the electric van in full at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, which runs from September 14 (press day) through September 20.
Ahead of its upcoming debut, Kia previewed the PV7 for the first time in a series of images and videos. While it’s still just a brief look, it’s pretty clear that the PV7 is noticeably longer than the PV5.
Kia PV7 preview (Source: Hyundai Motor Group)
Kia has yet to announce specific details, but we do know the PV7 will be based on the same modular E-GMP.S platform as the PV5.
The PV7 concept from CES 2024 measured 5,270 mm in length, 2,065 mm in width, and 2,120 mm in height, with a 3,390 mm wheelbase. That’s considerably bigger than the PV5 Passenger, measuring 4,695 mm in length, 1,895 mm in width, and 1,915 mm in height, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.
The official teasers confirm previous prototype sightings. Leading up to its debut, the PV7 has been
spotted several times
testing in public.
A few weeks ago, it was captured on a car carrier in Korea. In the video from
HealerTV
(watch below), the PV7’s wheelbase is nearly the same size as the truck it’s sitting on.
Like the PV5, the PV7 is expected to feature Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system and fleet management software.
Kia said the PV7 will deliver “a new mobility experience that caters to diverse customer needs, ranging from professional work environments to daily travel and leisure activities, by offering a spacious and flexible space.”
The larger electric van will be available in several configurations. In the preview, you can see Passenger and Cargo variants, like the PV5.
We will learn more details at the event in September. The PV7 will make its debut, while Kia will reveal future PBV plans and showcase new PV5 derivatives.
After it went on sale at the end of 2025, the PV5 has exceeded even Kia’s own expectations. As of August, Kia has sold over 39,000 PV5 vans. Will the larger PV7 see the same success?

title: EPA estimates vs. real-world data: EV drivers share some surprising experiences
content:
ev range
range anxiety
Jo Borrás
| Aug 31 2026 - 6:25 am PT
Electric cars are often marketed as having “x” miles of EPA-estimated range, but that doesn’t mean that’s how many miles you’ll be able to get out of yours. That’s the reality facing a growing number of Redditors who are sharing their EV commuting experiences online — and their real-world results might surprise you!
In a recent post to
r/electricvehicles
, a Redditor going by TallWall6378 shared that they weren’t seeing anything like their Ford E-Transit’s EPA-rated 116 miles of range per charge –
they were getting a lot more
“All summer I get 140 miles range in my 116 mile rated Ford E-transit due to my typical 40 mph windy road drive into town, with very little use of friction brakes,”
writes TallWall6378
. “And that’s with 1,800 pounds payload as my baseline (verified today on scales). So about 20% better than rated, but kind of an unusual vehicle.”
Van-tastic range
2024 E-Transit electric van; by Ford.
TallWall6378’s real-world range results are impressive – but they were quickly one-upped by another E-Transit owner going by
FlatDiscussion4649
. “I’m doing slightly better with the same vehicle @ 150 miles in summer (2.2 miles per Kw),” they wrote. “I always keep it in ‘eco’ mode and I try not to use more than 30% of the power available when accelerating. I drive about 60 miles per trip and at least 20 miles of that is at 60 mph, Probably another 20 miles at around 50 mph and the rest @ 30-40 mph.”
Other Redditors quickly piled on, sharing not only their anecdotal experiences but photos of their in-dash range guess-o-meters (GoMs) for additional back up and validation.
Range guess-o-meters
IndieMrToasty
That last GoM works out to about 5 miles of driving per kWh of battery capacity, and jifff’s description of their commute might sound pretty familiar to suburban parents. “Over 8km/kwh (5mi/kwh?),”
they write
, “my commute/suburb is mostly 30kmh zones with speed bumps and schools everywhere 😝”
Others piled on. “The EPA says my Kia does 240 miles on a charge,”
writes Traditional-Forum
. “In good weather I get 100 extra miles on a regular basis! Certainly some of it is driving style,
but it is widely reported that these early Kia EV’s are hyper efficient
My favorite personal EV range story, though, is the one shared by a user going by pimpbot666, who wrote about one of my personal favorites, the Volkswagen eGolf.
When my wife drives the ’19 eGolf to work, she comes back with some crazy numbers.
eGolf has 125 miles EPA rated range. We usually show around 135 miles on the guess-o-meter in moderate weather on a full charge after some average around town and a little freeway driving.
Her commute is 52 miles round trip, over a ridge that peaks 900 feet above sea level. The house is at 180 feet above sea level. This has a lot of stop and go traffic.
She leaves with 135 miles and comes home with …
110 miles on the guess-o-meter
. Average consumption shows up to 5.5mi/kWh when she commutes. Normally, we see around 4 to 4.5 miles/kWh.
The next day when we charge it back up to 100%, the guess-o-meter will show up to 155 miles, but drops fast in average driving.
PIMPBOT666
Taken altogether, these real-world snapshots prove that whether it’s an affordable VW eGolf or a late-model Lucid Air, EV drivers out in the real world are seeing range that’s meaningfully and measurably better than the EPA range estimates might suggest, underscoring the fact that those range estimates aren’t “ideal scenarios,” as many EV critics suggest, but rather exactly what it says on the tin:
estimates
What’s more, by the EPA’s own admission,
their range estimates are a bit conservative
. “The city and highway driving ranges determined from this testing are adjusted to account for real-world factors that are not represented on the laboratory test procedures,”
reads the EPA’s official explainer site
. “These factors include such things the impact of air conditioning, of cold temperatures, and of high speed and aggressive driving behavior. Although the regulations allow some optional approaches, the most common approach is to use a factor of
to adjust all the test parameters,
including range
. For example: An EV achieves 200 miles on the highway laboratory test.
Real-world highway driving range → 200 x 0.7 = 140 miles
to account for aggressive driving and HVAC use.”
What they’re getting at there is that (as ever) when it comes to efficiency,
it is often more important
you drive than
you drive
– and beating the EPA estimated range estimate isn’t just theoretically possible …
a lot of people are already doing it
How about you guys? Are your real-world range results better or worse than what the EPA thinks you’ll get, or are you making them look like chumps? Head on down to the comments and let us know.

title: Tesla confirms Autopilot/FSD was active in strange fatal crash
content:
Tesla told federal regulators that its driver-assist system was “verified engaged” when a Model 3 crashed at 104 mph and killed its driver in Clute, Texas — a detail that never appeared in any police statement or news report about the crash, which happened in May 2026.
The gap between Tesla’s own data and the public account of the crash is the latest example of how little the public learns about crashes involving the company’s Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” systems.
What Tesla reported to NHTSA
The crash appears in Tesla’s own filings to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration under the Standing General Order (SGO), which requires automakers to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed, injured, or the vehicle was towed.
We found it while analyzing the full SGO dataset, which now contains nearly 4,000 Tesla driver-assist crashes.
In the report, Tesla lists the vehicle as a 2025 Model 3 driven by a consumer, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s a step beyond the “unknown” or “reported” labels that appear on many records — it means Tesla confirmed, through its own telematics, that Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was active. The report also shows Tesla had telematics data available for the crash.
Tesla logged the vehicle’s pre-crash speed at 104 mph, on a road it categorized as a “Street,” and recorded the outcome as a fatality.
Then it redacted almost everything that would explain how those facts fit together. The crash narrative, the specific software version, and even the field indicating whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area are all blacked out as “confidential business information” — the same redactions Tesla applies to 99.9% of its crash reports. Because the software-version field is hidden, the public file cannot even confirm whether the system engaged was Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving.”
What police and the media said
The public account of the same crash contains none of that.
The driver was Steven Alvarez, 23, an IT technician at Lake Jackson Intermediate School and a Brazoswood High School graduate, according to Brazosport ISD, which mourned him publicly. Local outlets reported that on the afternoon of May 20, 2026, his car left Brazoswood Drive, crashed through a fence at Clute Municipal Park, and hit the complex of a decommissioned, empty pool, where it caught fire.
Clute police said their preliminary belief was that Alvarez had suffered a medical episode. No outlet mentioned Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any Tesla driver-assist system. And crucially, no police statement or news report cited a speed — the only public hint that speed was a factor was a single description of a “speeding Tesla” on social media. The 104 mph figure exists only in Tesla’s telematics.
What could have happened — and why we can’t tell
Tesla’s data confirms one thing: the driver-assist system was on. It does not, on its own, tell us what role the system played. Several possibilities are consistent with the redacted record.
The system could have been actively driving in a way that contributed to the crash. But Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” do not normally take a car to 104 mph on a residential street on their own, which points toward driver input.
Tesla’s speed figure could be wrong. SGO speed fields are self-reported and occasionally inconsistent, and 104 mph is extreme for the setting. It deserves independent verification against the police crash report and any physical evidence.
Or the police theory and Tesla’s data could both be right at once: Alvarez may have suffered a medical emergency and involuntarily pressed the accelerator while the system was engaged, pushing the car past any speed the software would command. That is close to what Tesla says happened in the fatal Katy, Texas crash, where it admits “Full Self-Driving” was on but blames the driver for flooring the accelerator to 73 mph.
The point is that the public cannot distinguish between these scenarios — and neither can investigators working only from the public file — because Tesla sealed the narrative, the software version, and the operating-area field.
Electrek’s Take
I want to be careful here, because a young man died and his family deserves accuracy, not a narrative. We do not know that Tesla’s driver-assist caused this crash. It’s entirely possible a medical emergency did, with the system a bystander.
Top comment by Rick Bungiro
It makes sense given Tesla’s overall “pay no attention to the man behind the curtain” strategy. One would think that if the software was running but played no significant role in the crash, Tesla would want to put all the data out there to prove it. But if they did, that naturally leads to the reasonable question of why they’re still hiding the details of other crashes.
Bottom line: Beware the person who claims to have invented a better mousetrap, but then makes it hard to figure out why it just killed the cat.
But that’s exactly the problem. Tesla holds the data that would answer the question, verified engagement, the telematics behind that 104 mph, the software version, the video, the driver-monitoring state, and it has chosen to black all of it out. The public was told this was likely a medical episode. Tesla’s own records say its automation was verified engaged in the crash. Both can’t be the whole story, and only Tesla can reconcile them.
This is the strongest argument for why the redactions have to end. When Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” is verified engaged in a fatal crash, “confidential business information” should not be allowed to bury what the car was doing. Tesla is already under NHTSA investigation over how it reports these crashes, and its own AI trainers have told Reuters they don’t trust its safety stats. A family in Clute is left with a police theory, while the company that sold the software sits on the data. That shouldn’t be Tesla’s call to make.
I strongly advocate that Tesla stop redacting crash data from NHTSA. We need to understand exactly how these automated systems are involved in crashes happening on public roads, especially as Tesla claims that it won’t require supervision soon.

title: Can REITs become a capital-recycling engine for renewables? - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China’s emerging renewable energy real estate investment trust (REIT) market could give developers a new way to recycle capital from operating solar assets into the next generation of projects.
Vincent Shaw
31 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
China’s first reported expansion of a clean REIT for inter-institutional investors has put a relatively uncommon financing structure in the spotlight: turning dozens of small commercial and industrial (C&I) solar plants into an investable product for long-term institutional capital.
PCG Power completed the first expansion of its “Xingzheng Jishi – Bicheng Nengfa New Energy Holding-type Real Estate Asset-backed Special Plan (Carbon Neutrality)” on Aug. 20. The product was established in December 2025 with around 130 MW of operating C&I distributed solar assets.
Following the expansion, the underlying portfolio had grown to about 400 MW, representing roughly CNY 1.5 billion ($209 million) of investment, while cumulative fundraising exceeded CNY 800 million.
The deal matters less for its absolute size than for the capital cycle it is attempting to establish. Renewable energy projects require large amounts of upfront capital but can remain in operation for 20 to 30 years. For developers that retain projects on their balance sheets, capital can therefore remain tied up for decades. Project finance helps build assets; securitization can help recycle the capital already embedded in them.
In theory, that creates a loop: develop, build, operate, securitize, reinvest – and build again.
Renewable energy securitization itself is not new. US residential solar loan-backed securities have developed into what ratings agency KBRA describes as a mainstream asset-backed securities (ABS) product. In Europe, listed vehicles such as The Renewables Infrastructure Group (TRIG) give investors exposure to portfolios of wind, solar, and storage assets. India has also used infrastructure investment trusts, including Virescent Renewable Energy Trust, whose initial portfolio comprised around 395 MW of operating solar projects.
REIT-style structures holding renewable infrastructure, however, remain far less common than property REITs, particularly for highly fragmented C&I solar portfolios. China’s “inter-institutional REITs” are also not identical to the listed public REITs familiar to international investors. In July, the Shanghai Stock Exchange formally defined the products as real estate asset-backed securities with equity characteristics, renaming what had previously been known as holding-type real estate ABS.
The harder question is why renewable energy assets, despite their long operating lives and potentially stable cash flows, have not fitted REIT structures as naturally as offices, warehouses, or shopping centers.
PCG’s portfolio illustrates one answer: standardization.
Samuel Yan, president and CFO of PCG Power, told pv magazine that the projects in the company’s first portfolio averaged only around 3 MW each. The initial 130 MW pool comprised roughly 40 to 50 projects, while the expansion added more than 200 MW and another 50 to 60 projects across multiple provinces and industries.
Unlike a property REIT holding several large buildings, a distributed solar vehicle may therefore have to manage dozens or even hundreds of small assets. Each rooftop can differ in ownership documentation, structural loading, commercial contracts, power consumption patterns, and counterparty credit.
PCG has sought to address that problem by standardizing assets before they reach the capital market. Yan said the company applies “red-line” criteria that can disqualify a project outright, including property compliance and structural safety requirements, alongside “yellow-line” criteria under which additional returns may compensate for manageable, non-standard risks. The company then applies standardized engineering procedures, a unified operations and maintenance (O&M) platform, and common long-term operating rules.
The implication is that the financial product cannot be standardized unless the physical assets are standardized first.
There is a second challenge. A REIT platform is not simply another way for a developer to package several projects, sell them, and walk away. It requires a continuing pipeline of new assets, long-term operations, repeat expansions, and sustained cash-flow quality.
Yan said this distinguishes the model from the traditional develop-build-sell approach used by many renewable energy developers. In effect, it could turn a renewable energy developer from an asset seller into an asset manager, favoring companies that combine development, construction, O&M, power trading, and financial asset management.
China is an unusually large test bed for that model. Distributed PV capacity had reached 576 GW by the end of June 2026, according to the National Energy Administration. Meanwhile, China is formalizing a multi-layer REIT market. The Shanghai Stock Exchange said in July that inter-institutional REIT issuance across 15 asset categories, including renewable infrastructure, had already approached CNY 100 billion.
Still, REITs are unlikely to become a universal answer to renewable energy finance. Assets generally need established operating cash flows before securitization. Fragmented portfolios carry high due diligence and management costs, while electricity prices, power purchase agreement performance, curtailment, degradation, and customer credit create risks that differ substantially from property rents. Tax treatment and eligible-asset rules also vary between jurisdictions.
The more realistic role for REITs is therefore as an additional exit and capital-recycling channel alongside bank lending, project finance, infrastructure funds, and conventional ABS.
The real test of PCG’s experiment is not whether one solar REIT can be issued. It is whether portfolios can repeatedly absorb new assets and attract long-term capital. If they can, securitization could turn operating renewable energy plants from a destination for capital into a source of capital for the next generation of projects.

content:
Research & Development
Novventos Clean Energy has developed a container-based hybrid system combining modular photovoltaics with small vertical-axis wind turbines for off-grid and temporary applications.
Petra Hannen,
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
31 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
The system is designed to supply decentralized electricity for off-grid and temporary applications
Austrian startup Novventos Clean Energy has developed a container-based hybrid power system combining photovoltaics with small vertical-axis wind turbines. The system is designed to supply decentralized electricity for off-grid and temporary applications, with a common energy management system controlling both generation technologies.
Modular PV system for ISO containers
Founded in 2023, Novventos Clean Energy has developed the “sky.boost” PV system with a modular architecture designed for installation on ISO containers. According to the company, the system can be assembled within a few hours.
The second generation component is the “naca.boost,” a small vertical-axis wind turbine designed for installation at heights of 3 meters to 8 meters. The manufacturer says the turbine can harness turbulent airflow close to the ground, where conventional wind turbines may be less suitable.
A fairing directs the wind toward the rotor. The wind component is intended to complement PV generation during periods of low solar irradiance. According to Novventos, two naca.boost turbines can generate 12,000 kWh of electricity, while the PV component produces an average of 3,400 kWh. The company does not specify the period over which these generation figures apply.
Shared management system for solar and wind
The PV and wind components are controlled by the company’s “master.boost” energy management system, which monitors the output of both technologies and manages energy distribution.
Generation and operating data are also centralized on the company’s cloud platform and can be accessed through a web-based interface.
Novventos combines the components in a container-based system marketed as “mobile.energy.” The company says the system is intended for off-grid locations and temporary applications and can also be supplied with an optional trailer.
Limited technical data available
Novventos has not provided detailed technical specifications for the complete system. In particular, the company does not state the installed PV or wind power capacity, making it difficult to assess the stated electricity-generation figures.
The company also does not mention battery storage as part of the mobile.energy system.

title: Global solar O&M market reaches 348 GW as consolidation accelerates - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The global solar PV O&M market reached 348 GW in 2025, with the 15 largest providers controlling 57% of managed capacity as consolidation accelerated. NovaSource remained the global leader, while rapid portfolio growth reshaped provider rankings and regional markets.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
31 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
The global solar PV operations and maintenance (O&M) market reached 348 GW at the end of 2025, after adding 61 GW during the year. The expansion came amid accelerating industry consolidation, with the 15 largest providers managing 200 GW, or 57% of the capacity analyzed.
The figures come from Wood Mackenzie’s “Global Solar PV O&M Service Provider Dynamics 2026” report, which examines portfolio sizes, cost trends and service strategies among more than 130 active providers across the Americas, Asia-Pacific excluding China, and Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
Consolidation accelerated in 2025, with the 15 largest providers adding a combined 41 GW to their portfolios to reach 200 GW of managed capacity. NovaSource Power Services retained its position as the world’s largest solar PV O&M provider, with 38.4 GW under management at the end of the year.
RES Energy Global Services, Solv Energy, Solarig Energy Services and Recurrent Energy retained their positions among the five largest providers globally. Several are pursuing cross-regional expansion strategies as scale becomes an increasingly important competitive factor.
The rankings also saw new entrants. BayWa r.e. Services and Origis Energy Services joined the global top 15 after adding 2.6 GW and 1.8 GW, respectively, to their managed portfolios.
Engie more than doubled its O&M portfolio in 2025, rising six places to rank eighth globally. Growth was driven primarily by the Americas, where its portfolio expanded by 172%.
Sterling & Wilson recorded 53% year-on-year growth, taking its managed capacity to 13.5 GW and placing it sixth globally. The company also leads the Asia-Pacific market, where it manages 12.2 GW.
Among smaller providers, megaom, the independent O&M unit of FRV, recorded the strongest percentage growth. Its portfolio expanded by 243% to 3.8 GW, taking the company into the global top 30 for the first time.
Regional markets showed markedly different trends. Wood Mackenzie described North America as a mature and highly competitive market, with pricing pressure pushing down the cost of comprehensive O&M services. Prices for “full-wrap” contracts fell 18% year on year.

title: U.S. startup exceeds 10% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency with 100 cm² module - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
SunHydrogen has achieved solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiencies above 10% with its 100 cm² modules in tests at Sparc Hydrogen’s laboratories. The U.S. company is now targeting efficiencies approaching 15% while working to scale the technology to larger, manufacturable modules.
Lior Kahana
31 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Hydrogen
The company’s commercial-size 1.92m² hydrogen module
Iowa-headquartered photoelectrochemical technology company SunHydrogen has achieved solar-to-hydrogen (STH) conversion efficiencies of more than 10% with its 100 cm² hydrogen modules during preliminary testing at Sparc Hydrogen’s laboratories, according to a company statement.
The latest performance follows earlier testing of SunHydrogen’s 100 cm² modules at the R&D facilities of Japanese automaker Honda, where the devices achieved an active-area STH efficiency of 10.8%. Honda and SunHydrogen have been working under a joint development agreement aimed at advancing the technology toward an installation-ready hydrogen panel and cost-effective commercial production.
“SunHydrogen’s system is an integrated semiconductor-electrocatalyst architecture in which the light-absorbing semiconductor, purpose-designed contacts and water-splitting catalysts are engineered to operate together as a single hydrogen-generating module,” SunHydrogen Business Director Tor Erik Hoftun told
pv magazine
. “When sunlight is absorbed, the semiconductor generates electrons and holes. Purpose-designed contacts route these photogenerated charge carriers to integrated hydrogen- and oxygen-evolution catalysts. The electrons drive the production of hydrogen, while the holes drive the production of oxygen.”
Unlike a conventional PV module, whose cell layout and electrical contacts are designed primarily to deliver power to an external circuit, such as a separate electrolyzer stack, SunHydrogen’s semiconductor module is engineered specifically for direct solar-to-hydrogen conversion.
“In PV terms, the semiconductor’s current-voltage characteristics are matched to the electrochemical load so that the coupled module operates at a point that maximizes the conversion of incident solar energy into chemical energy stored in hydrogen,” Hoftun said.
“The hydrogen-generating module operates inside a reactor housing that manages electrolyte circulation and the collection and handling of the hydrogen and oxygen produced,” he added. “Because the photovoltaic and electrochemical functions are directly coupled, the architecture does not require a separate electrolyzer stack and can avoid much of the power-conversion equipment normally used. At the pilot and system level, auxiliary balance-of-system components are still used for electrolyte circulation, gas handling, monitoring, controls and safety.”
Following the recent test results, SunHydrogen entered into an agreement with Australia-based Sparc Hydrogen, which is developing a process that uses concentrated sunlight, water and a photocatalyst to produce hydrogen without an electrolyzer. The companies plan to assess the integration of SunHydrogen’s modules into Sparc Hydrogen’s reactors, with the aim of reducing hydrogen production costs.
“Under the 24-month Sparc Hydrogen collaboration, laboratory testing under concentrated sunlight is expected to progress, subject to technical milestones, to on-sun testing at Sparc Hydrogen’s Sharp facility in South Australia and an assessment of levelized hydrogen cost, with a potential pathway to a module-supply or manufacturing-license agreement,” Hoftun said.
He added that SunHydrogen is working with CTF Solar and other manufacturing partners to support the development of higher-efficiency products with Honda R&D.
In addition to testing at the 100 cm² scale, SunHydrogen has achieved efficiencies approaching 9% with a 1.92 m², PV-sized development module in outdoor testing.
“Subject to extension of the joint development program with Honda R&D, the next development phase is expected to advance the module architecture toward active-area solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies approaching 15%, with a focus on translating higher efficiency to larger, manufacturable modules,” Hoftun said.

title: Storing renewables with firebrick thermal batteries - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Electrified Thermal Solutions is developing a firebrick-based thermal battery that converts low-cost electricity into high-temperature heat for energy-intensive industries. The technology could pair with solar and wind to absorb surplus generation and deliver round-the-clock industrial heat at costs competitive with natural gas.
Lior Kahana
31 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
An E-brick
Rapid growth in data centers, industrial production, and economy-wide electrification is straining power systems worldwide. At the same time, manufacturers of steel, cement, chemicals, and other materials remain largely dependent on fossil fuels to provide the high-temperature process heat they need.
Electrified Thermal Solutions
, a Boston-based startup, is developing a thermal storage system designed to electrify heavy industry while limiting strain on the grid. The company’s Joule Hive Thermal Battery (JHTB), also known as the E-brick, combines traditional firebricks with advanced firebricks that conduct electricity. The bricks serve three functions within the system: heating elements, thermal storage media, and heat exchangers.
The system allows high-temperature industrial facilities to store off-peak electricity as heat and, on demand, release that heat as hot air through channels in the bricks to furnaces, kilns, or boilers. Electrified Thermal Solutions says the E-brick is compatible with electrical supplies ranging from 480 V to 100 kV and can store heat at temperatures of up to 1,800 C. Output temperatures can be adjusted from 200 C to 1,800 C.
“We believe we are on track to deliver the lowest-cost, highest-value thermal battery on the market. For a thermal battery, the honest metric is the levelized cost of heat (LCOH), because our product is hot gas delivered to a furnace, displacing natural gas or other polluting fuels. And that cost is dominated by one variable: the price of the electricity you charge with,” Daniel Stack, CEO and co-founder of Electrified Thermal Solutions, told
pv magazine
The Joule Hive Thermal Battery at Southwest Research Institute | Image: Electrified Thermal Solutions
“The Joule Hive converts and stores power as heat at greater than 98% efficiency, and the storage medium is essentially a brick. Hence, the capital adder on top of the electricity is small,” he added. “That means LCOH depends on three things: how cheaply you can buy power, the temperature and duration of the heat you deliver, and the size of the system, since larger installations store more energy per dollar of material. Today we can beat natural gas anywhere in the world where its delivered price is above €30 ($34.8)/MWh on a subsidy-free basis.”
“Every charge cycle of our first commercial-scale system is, in effect, a solar test,” Stack added. “It charges directly from the Texas grid, where solar and wind routinely set the price – including the negative-price hours we deliberately target. The bricks don’t care where the electrons come from: an AC grid connection, a co-located array, or both.”
Stack said thermal storage could be particularly valuable in markets with high levels of solar generation.
“In solar-heavy grids, where midday prices regularly go negative, a thermal battery is exactly the flexible load the system is begging for – it turns curtailed solar into useful energy,” he said. “For factories: pairing on-site PV with a Joule Hive lets a plant oversize its solar relative to its grid connection and convert the midday surplus into firm, 24/7 industrial heat.”
The company, founded in 2022, commissioned its first 20 MWh commercial system earlier this year at the Southwest Research Institute in San Antonio, Texas. To date, Electrified Thermal Solutions has raised $24.3 million across six funding rounds.

title: India adds 6.6 GW of rooftop solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Q2 installations reached 3.8 GW, up 41% quarter-on-quarter and 136% year-on-year
Uma Gupta
31 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
A residential solar installation by SolarSquare
India installed 6.6 GW of rooftop solar capacity in the first half of calendar year 2026, up 136% compared to the 2.8 GW installed in H1 2025, according to Mercom India’s newly released Q2 and 1H 2026 India Rooftop Solar Market Report.
The figure includes 3.8 GW of rooftop solar capacity added in the second quarter, up 41% from the 2.7 GW installed in Q1 2026. Q2 installations also increased 136% year on year from 1.6 GW in Q2 2025.
Rooftop solar accounted for 33% of India’s total solar installations during the quarter.
According to Mercom, rooftop solar installations were primarily driven by the Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (PM Surya Ghar program). Rooftop systems had been installed in nearly 4.5 million households by June 2026, reaching approximately 45% of the program’s target of 10 million households.
Residential installations continued to dominate the market in Q2 2026, contributing 84% of total additions. Industrial installations accounted for 10%, followed by commercial installations at 5%, and government installations at 1%.
Installations under the capex model accounted for a majority of quarterly additions in Q2 2026.
The implementation of ALMM List-II requirements from June 1, 2026, increased pressure on domestic cell availability and domestic content requirement (DCR) module prices. Subsequent transition measures eased near-term pressure, with eligible net-metering and open access projects receiving a transition window until Dec. 31, 2026. Residential consumers under PM Surya Ghar opting for the “Give It Up” category can forgo the subsidy and use non-DCR modules until the program ends in March 2027.
“India has a strong residential rooftop solar pipeline, but converting it into installations will depend on faster approvals, financing, and project delivery. Higher grid tariffs should strengthen commercial demand, but rising system costs and regulatory constraints could limit industrial growth,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO of Mercom Capital Group. “The ALMM transition window will help projects move forward in the second half, but it could also trigger a rush to meet deadlines and increase price volatility. Beyond 2026, market growth will depend on domestic cell capacity ramping up quickly and states removing approval, metering, and grid connectivity bottlenecks.”

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: Another 5 major solar manufacturers announce H1 losses - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Longi, TCL Zhonghuan, GCL Technology, Daqo and Xinte Energy remained in the red, despite signs of operational stabilization.
Vincent Shaw
31 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Shenzhen Stock Exchange
China’s leading solar manufacturers remained under heavy financial pressure in the first half of 2026, as persistent oversupply and weak prices continued to weigh on the polysilicon, wafer and module segments.
Results from Longi, TCL Zhonghuan, GCL Technology, Daqo New Energy and Xinte Energy indicate that profitability has yet to recover materially across much of the upstream and integrated solar supply chain. Operating trends are beginning to diverge, however, with some companies reporting narrower losses, stronger cash flow, or growth in overseas and non-PV businesses.
reported first-half revenue of CNY 27.05 billion, down 17.6% year on year, while its net loss attributable to shareholders widened 43.4% to CNY 3.68 billion. Operating cash flow swung to an outflow of CNY 5.82 billion. The company shipped 48.91 GW of wafers, including 18.98 GW to external customers, and 29.93 GW of modules. Overseas module sales rose by more than 26%, with international markets accounting for more than 65% of module revenue. Longi attributed its losses to continued oversupply, low capacity utilization, higher silver costs and foreign exchange effects. It also signed more than 3 GWh of energy storage orders during the period.
TCL Zhonghuan
showed clearer signs of stabilization. Revenue increased 6.8% to CNY 14.31 billion, while its net loss narrowed 24.5% to CNY 3.20 billion. Operating cash flow remained positive at CNY 321 million. Wafer shipments reached 53.9 GW, while module shipments rose 29% year on year. Revenue from cells and modules increased by about 47% to CNY 5.29 billion, reflecting the company’s shift toward a more integrated product portfolio. Overseas markets accounted for around 25% of revenue.
Upstream polysilicon producers remained under greater pressure.
GCL Technology
recorded revenue of CNY 5.78 billion, broadly flat year on year, while its attributable net loss widened 17.2% to CNY 2.08 billion. Its gross loss, however, narrowed 38.1% to CNY 434 million. The company had 480,000 metric tons of annual granular polysilicon production capacity at the end of June. Its average external selling price was CNY 31.97/kg, compared with an average cash production cost of CNY 25.23/kg. GCL is also diversifying into new materials, with a 200,000-metric-ton lithium iron phosphate cathode material plant starting production in June.
Daqo New Energy
reported the steepest revenue decline among the five companies. First-half revenue fell 57.6% to CNY 623 million, while its attributable net loss widened 39.1% to CNY 1.60 billion. Polysilicon production rose 71.3% to 87,077 metric tons, but sales fell 57.4% to 19,672 metric tons as Daqo restricted deliveries amid depressed prices. Its average selling price fell to CNY 30.63/kg, below its cash production cost of CNY 34.75/kg. The company booked around CNY 1.03 billion in inventory impairment charges but retained approximately CNY 10.42 billion in cash and cash-like assets, with no interest-bearing debt.
Xinte Energy
reported the strongest improvement among the five companies. Revenue rose 38.9% to CNY 10.15 billion, while its attributable net loss narrowed 17.3% to CNY 212 million. Gross margin increased to 13.13% from 9.14%, while operating cash flow turned positive at CNY 84 million. Polysilicon revenue nearly quadrupled to CNY 3.89 billion on higher sales volumes, while wind and solar project construction contributed CNY 3.40 billion. Revenue from electrical equipment, including energy storage systems, rose 8.9% to CNY 1.59 billion.
Taken together, the results show that China’s solar manufacturing sector remains caught between excess production capacity and weak pricing. Longi, GCL Technology and Daqo remained deeply in the red, while TCL Zhonghuan and Xinte Energy showed clearer signs of stabilization.
The results also point to a broader strategic shift, with leading manufacturers placing greater emphasis on cash flow, overseas sales, product mix and diversification rather than shipment growth alone. Although some operating indicators are improving, a broad recovery in profitability across China’s solar manufacturing sector has yet to materialize.

title: Journey Ahead: JA Roadshow 2026 to spotlight integrated energy solutions - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
As energy resilience rises on the agenda across Europe, JA’s first roadshow, Journey Ahead: JA Roadshow 2026, will bring the company’s expanding PV and energy storage portfolio directly to customers, demonstrating how integrated technologies can support greater grid resilience and meet evolving energy needs.
31 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Grid instability, growing electrification, and rising demand for energy resilience are reshaping Europe’s energy landscape. As developers, installers, EPCs, and asset owners seek solutions that go beyond power generation alone, integrated approaches combining solar and energy storage are becoming increasingly important.
Against this backdrop, JA will launch
Journey Ahead: JA Roadshow 2026
, an initiative designed to bring the company’s latest technology developments directly to customers and industry stakeholders across Europe. The roadshow will serve as a mobile showcase of JA’s expanding energy ecosystem, giving visitors direct access to JA experts and the company’s latest innovations.
A key focus of the tour will be battery energy storage systems (BESS). As energy markets evolve and grid constraints become more visible, storage is emerging as a critical technology for improving flexibility, increasing self-consumption, managing peak demand, and strengthening energy security. Product demonstrations and technical discussions will focus on how storage can support more resilient and reliable energy systems.
Among the solutions on display will be JAPlanet 2.0, JAPlanet Fusion, and JAGalaxy, showcasing JA’s growing presence across C&I and utility-scale storage. Together, these solutions reflect the company’s broader vision of delivering integrated energy systems that combine generation, storage, and intelligent energy management.
The roadshow will also feature a selection of JA’s latest PV technologies, highlighting the company’s continued focus on performance, reliability, and application-driven innovation.
Visitors will have the opportunity to explore products from JA’s latest-generation TOPCon platform, DeepBlue 5.0, including JAM48D50/LR and JAM66D50/GB. The exhibition will also present the DeepBlue 4.0 Pro TOPCon portfolio, represented by JAM54D40/LR and JAM66D45/LB, featuring JA’s anti-glare solutions with both microstructured glass and acid-etched glass variants. Completing the lineup is the new HyperGen module JAT54S4F/GR, JA’s new back-contact technology with world-record certified cell conversion efficiency of 28.2%.
The event reflects JA’s continued evolution from a leading PV manufacturer into an integrated energy solutions provider. By combining high-efficiency modules, energy storage technologies, and application-focused innovation, JA is expanding its offering to address changing energy needs across Europe.
The roadshow will kick off in Poland on 2 September before continuing through Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Slovenia, Italy, Austria, Germany, Spain, Belgium, and the Netherlands. As the itinerary develops, the latest locations, schedules, and updates will be published on the dedicated
roadshow microsite
. The platform will serve as a central hub for information throughout the tour, ensuring attendees can stay informed as new stops and activities are announced.

title: Denmark adds 337 MW of solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Denmark installed more solar during the first half of 2026 than it did during the first half of 2025, with market growth currently driven by larger-scale projects.
Patrick Jowett
31 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Denmark installed 336.7 MW of solar during the first half of the year (H1), according to figures published by Danish solar association Dansk Solcelleforening.
The figure is an 11% increase on deployments across the first half of 2025. Dansk Solcelleforening latest update says Denmark’s cumulative PV capacity now stands at 5.4 GW.
The association’s analysis says growth in Denmark’s solar market is currently driven by larger-scale projects. A total 271 MW of utility-scale solar, consisting projects larger than 1 MW, were switched on in H1 in Denmark, compared to 208 MW in the first half of 2025.
“Investment appetite remains high once projects have received regulatory approval and grid connection, which is a positive market signal,” a briefing published by the association says.
In contrast, the expansion of solar energy on buildings continues to decline across both the residential and C&I market segments in Denmark. Residential solar installations fell from 36.3 MW in the first half of 2025 to 28.2 MW in the first half of 2026, while C&I deployments fell from 55.2 MW to 37.2 MW across the same periods.
Dansk Solcelleforening added that the C&I downturn is particularly worrying, with the framework conditions for decentralized energy plants currently not attractive enough in a market with low energy prices.
“The segments that can relieve the electricity grid most effectively are developing the weakest,” the association explained. “In other words, the political ambitions have not yet been translated into framework conditions that raise the level of investments in solar power on buildings.”
Dansk Solcelleforening’s Birgitte Eskildsen told
pv magazine
that the Danish Parliament is preparing to implement new regulations that will make it “simpler and more attractive” to install PV on public buildings, expected to enter into force on September 14.
“Moreover, we expect the new government to come up with more initiatives, so that the amount of solar deployed will rise,” Eskildsen added.
During this year’s Intersolar in Munich,
pv magazine
met with Dansk Solcelleforening board members Johan Christensen and Jacob Engdal to
discuss the latest developments
in Denmark’s solar and storage markets.
